explanations.explanation: That's the lesson he picks up. The lament says, “After learning to tear his prey…” and then it tells where that leads. Some kids learn to ride a bike. This young lion learned something a lot rougher. Keep your eye on him, friend, because the nations are paying attention too.

No guarding in this verse, friend. The lament says the cub became a young lion, and then, “After learning to tear his prey, he devoured men.” That's a heavy line, and I won't pretend otherwise. What he learns is tearing his prey, not watching over anybody.

Hiding isn't what this cub is about, baker. The text says he became a young lion and learned to tear his prey. It says nothing here about him ducking anybody. If anything, the nations hear about him, and that's where his trouble starts.

Right, baker. The lament says, “When the nations heard of him, he was trapped in their pit.” Word got around about this lion, and the nations had a pit ready. Nobody here is handing out a welcome basket. Then they lead him off with hooks to Egypt.

No crown in this verse, friend. When the nations heard of him, he was trapped in their pit. After that, hooks led him away to the land of Egypt. Nobody throws a coronation for a lion they just dropped in a pit.

explanations.answer: He drives them from their land
explanations.explanation: This lion doesn't get to push anybody out. The lament says the nations heard of him and he was trapped in their pit. They don't run from him, they catch him. Then hooks lead him away to the land of Egypt, baker.

True, baker. The text says that when she saw she had waited in vain and her hope was lost, she took another of her cubs and made him a young lion. So the lament doesn't stop at one cub. She tries again with another. Hang on to that, because this second cub gets a whole stretch of the lament to himself.

It's actually true, friend. The text says she saw that she had waited in vain, that her hope was lost. Then she took another of her cubs and made him a young lion. So she does go on, and the second cub is up next.

That's the word, baker. The lament says, “He broke down their strongholds and devastated their cities.” Strongholds are fortified places, so he's going after the sturdy stuff first. This is a lion who doesn't knock before he enters. And the whole land notices.

Nothing gets rebuilt in this verse, friend. The text says he broke down their strongholds and devastated their cities. It's the opposite of a construction crew. The land and everything in it shuddered at the sound of his roaring (Ezekiel 19:7).

No guarding in this verse, baker. The lament says he broke down their strongholds and devastated their cities. A stronghold is a fortified place, and he's the one knocking them down. So this young lion is no protector of cities.

A net, baker. The text says the nations “spread their net over him; he was trapped in their pit.” They came from the provinces on every side, so this was no lone hunter. Roar all you want, a net doesn't care. It's a net-and-pit combo.

A cloak is for staying warm, friend, and nobody's tucking this lion in. The text says the nations spread their net over him. Then he was trapped in their pit. That's the whole plan, and it's not a cozy one.

No banners in this verse, baker. The lament says the nations set out against him from the provinces on every side. Then they spread their net over him, and he was trapped in their pit. It's a trap, not a parade.

Yes, baker. The lament says, “With hooks they caged him and brought him to the king of Babylon.” So this time the destination is Babylon, not Egypt like the first cub. Hooks, a cage, and a long trip. It's a rough ride for a lion.
Moab isn't in this verse, friend. The text says the nations caged him with hooks and brought him to the king of Babylon. Babylon is the name to remember here. It's where he ends up in captivity.

Assyria isn't named here, baker. The lament says, “With hooks they caged him and brought him to the king of Babylon.” That's where the second lion is taken into captivity. Keep Babylon in your pocket, because it's the one the text gives.

It's the other way around, friend. The text says they brought him into captivity “so that his roar was heard no longer on the mountains of Israel.” The roar that made the whole land shudder is gone from those mountains. It's a quiet ending to a loud lion.

False is right, baker. The lament says he was taken into captivity so that his roar was “heard no longer on the mountains of Israel.” The same roar that made the land shudder has gone silent there. That's a big change for a lion who once filled the whole place with noise.

That's the picture, baker. The lament says the vine “was fruitful and full of branches because of the abundant waters.” It's planted by the water, and it shows. Think of a plant that gets everything it needs and just goes for it.

explanations.answer: Small and hidden in the shade
explanations.explanation: This vine isn't tucked away, friend. The text says it was fruitful and full of branches because of the abundant waters. Later it even towers high above the thick branches (Ezekiel 19:11). Nothing shy about it.

That's a sad little plant, baker, and it isn't this one. The lament says the vine was planted by the water, and it was fruitful and full of branches. Bare and thorny is not the description. This vine starts out thriving.

Not quite, friend. The text says the vine “towered high above the thick branches, conspicuous for its height and for its dense foliage.” So it doesn't hide, it sticks out. Plenty of people would pay good money for that kind of confidence.
False is right, baker. The lament says the vine towered high above the thick branches. It was conspicuous for its height and for its dense foliage. This one is standing out, not staying low.

explanations.answer: The east wind dries it up
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The lament says the vine was uprooted in fury and cast down to the ground, and “the east wind dried up its fruit.” So the fruit doesn't get taken, it just dries out. It's like a batch left on the counter with the oven off and the window open all week. No one's eating that one.
No birds in this verse, friend. The text says the east wind dried up its fruit. The vine was already uprooted and cast down to the ground. The fruit dries up right there with it.
Nobody comes along to gather it, baker. The lament says the vine was uprooted in fury and cast down to the ground. Then the east wind dried up its fruit. Nobody's picking it up.

True, baker. The lament says the vine's strong branches were stripped off and they withered, and then, “the fire consumed them.” First they dry out, then the fire finishes the job. It's a hard picture, and I think it's meant to be.
It's true, friend. The text says the strong branches were stripped off and they withered. Then it says, “the fire consumed them.” That's where those branches end up.

Yes, baker. The lament says, “Now it is planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land.” Remember where it started: planted by abundant waters. Now it's a dry and thirsty land. That's a long way from the water.
No walls in this verse, friend. The text says it's now planted in the wilderness, in a dry and thirsty land. A city with walls sounds like an upgrade. This is the opposite.

A mountain would be a nice view, baker, but that's not where it is. The lament says the vine is now planted in the wilderness. It's a dry and thirsty land. Back in verse 10 it was by the water, so that's quite a drop.

That's what the fire takes, baker. The lament says, “Fire has gone out from its main branch and devoured its fruit.” The fire starts at the main branch and the fruit goes with it. It's a rough ending for a vine that began so fruitful.
No wall gets mentioned here, friend. The text says fire has gone out from its main branch and devoured its fruit. The vine's own fruit is what's lost. Nothing about the vineyard wall.

Roots aren't what the text names, baker. The lament says fire went out from the main branch and devoured its fruit. That's the part that burns. The verse ends with no strong branch remaining fit for a ruler's scepter.
